newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF seeks more guarantees before Bulgaria accord.
newsitem.headline: IMF seeks more guarantees before Bulgaria accord.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund envoy said on Wednesday he needed assurances that the new Bulgarian government to be elected next month would follow the policies set out in any agreement reached now.

"I need to be convinced of a widespread agreement on the continuity of policies in the programme. This is what we will be trying to ascertain over the next few days," IMF Europe One department director Michael Deppler told reporters.
"I am hopeful that we can arrive at an arrangement, but we have not," said Deppler, who arrived in Sofia on Tuesday.

IMF negotiators started talks with Bulgaria's interim government last month on a funding agreement linked to implementation of a fixed exchange rate system to help stabilise the crumbling economy and repay foreign debts.

Speaking after meeting President Petar Stoyanov, Deppler said they had agreed on all general policies, but he needed assurances that the new government to take office after the April 19 general election would be committed to the reform programme being agreed now.
"I am also equally concerned about a clear commitment and the continuity of policies on these issues that are important," said Deppler.
He said he planned to seek guarantees of continuity in meetings with the main political parties.

The favourite to win a majority in the new parliament is the Union of Democratic Forces and its coalition allies, whose mass protests ousted the ex-communist Socialist government in February two years before the end of its term.
The UDF has shown clear commitment to market reform, liberalisation of trade rules and accelerated privatisation, all needed to haul the country out from economic collapse.
But disagreements with the Fund over practical steps still remain.

"There are still some points on which there is need for agreement, there are points for which there is no agreement, and there is also a need for the Fund to be assured of the continuity of policies," said Deppler.
Different approaches to bank privatisation are one of the setbacks that is halting the agreement, said a local banker, who declined to be named.
The IMF recommends to sell four ailing banks by year-end and seek reputable foreign institutions to manage two other big state banks.
But local bankers would like loans to re-capitalise the ailing banks and then offer them to investors.

The agreement, which Bulgarians officials still hope to sign by the end of this week, would include the interim government's programme on how to solve the grave banking and currency crisis, and this year's budget and structural reform plans.
The programme will also contain legal amendments to bank laws designed jointly with the IMF to enable the introduction of a currency board in June.

The currency board system would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank, thus preventing the printing of money.
Deppler, who plans to stay until the end of this week, said there were no practical obstacles in reaching a funding agreement with the interim cabinet by April. -- Sofia Newsroom 3592 981 4145
